title: Surface Chemistry and Catalysis: Where Reactions Really Happen

questions.question: Water vapour held on the surface of silica gel is an example of:
questions.rationale: Silica gel concentrates water molecules on its surface only - adsorption. Absorption would mean penetration into the bulk, as with anhydrous CaCl2, which first absorbs and then dissolves the water.

questions.question: Which statement about adsorption is correct?
questions.rationale: Gas molecules lose freedom (entropy decreases) when they stick to a surface; since adsorption is spontaneous at suitable conditions, delta-G must be negative, which forces delta-H negative. Adsorption is always exothermic.

questions.question: The enthalpy of chemisorption is typically:
questions.rationale: Chemisorption forms chemical bonds, so its enthalpy (80-240 kJ/mol) approaches reaction energies. Physisorption relies on weak van der Waals forces at roughly 20-40 kJ/mol.

questions.question: According to the Freundlich isotherm, x/m varies with pressure as:
questions.rationale: The empirical Freundlich law is x/m = kP^(1/n) with n > 1. It behaves linearly (x/m proportional to P) at very low pressure and saturates at very high pressure, which is exactly where the law fails.

questions.question: A catalyst changes the reaction rate by:
options: Lowering the activation energy via an alternative path
Shifting the equilibrium position toward products
Increasing the enthalpy change of the reaction
questions.rationale: A catalyst offers a route of lower activation energy so more molecules can react, and it emerges unchanged. It does not alter the equilibrium constant or the enthalpy - equilibrium is simply reached faster from either side.

questions.question: Molybdenum oxide added with iron in the Haber process is an example of:
questions.rationale: Mo2O3 does not catalyse ammonia synthesis itself but enhances the activity of the iron catalyst - a promoter. Poisons do the reverse (arsenic blocks iron's active sites), and inhibitors slow reactions.

questions.question: The Tyndall effect is shown by:
questions.rationale: Colloid particles (1-1000 nm) are comparable in size to the wavelength of light, so they scatter it and make the beam path visible. True-solution particles are far too small to scatter appreciably.

questions.question: For coagulating a negative sol such as As2S3, the most effective ion is:
questions.rationale: By the Hardy-Schulze rule the coagulating ion must carry the charge opposite to the sol (positive here), and higher charge works best: Al3+ > Ba2+ > Na+. Cl- has the wrong sign entirely.

questions.question: Milk is an example of:
questions.rationale: Milk is fat (liquid) dispersed in water (liquid) - an emulsion. Aerosols disperse in gas (fog), foams are gas-in-liquid (whipped cream), and gels are liquid-in-solid (jelly).

questions.question: Froth floatation concentration of sulphide ores depends on:
options: Preferential adsorption of collectors making ore particles water-repellent
Absorption of water into the ore
questions.rationale: Pine-oil collectors adsorb on sulphide particles, making them hydrophobic so they attach to air bubbles and rise with the froth, while wettable gangue sinks. It is adsorption - a surface phenomenon - doing the separation.
